senses.definition: A temporary support that is removed once the real system works on its own.
senses.caution: It tells people the thing is temporary, and they will later ask when it is being removed. For a rough first version of the real work, say draft instead.
senses.example: The manual review step is scaffolding. Once the classifier is calibrated it comes out.

cues.text: You hardcoded a lookup to unblock a demo and want your tech lead to know it is not meant to survive.
A sponsor asks why an automated pipeline still has a person in the middle of it, and you explain that the person is a temporary support who goes once the pipeline works alone.
A friend is propping up a bookshelf with a stack of magazines until the brackets arrive.
You are running alongside your daughter's bike with a hand under the saddle, and someone asks how long you plan to keep doing that.

distractors: An isolated environment where code runs without touching anything real.
A rig that drives a system from outside to see how it behaves.
Lasting only briefly, and created for one use before being thrown away.
A basic building block a platform hands you and expects you to compose things out of.
The preparation done in advance of a moment where a gap would cost you dearly.

senses.gloss: code that runs an AI agent
gloss_distractors: a contract with an outside vendor
the training data for a model
senses.definition: The software around an AI model that runs it, calls its tools and manages each step.
senses.caution: Testers may hear a test harness, so say agent harness when it matters. Keep it for the code around the model, and call the model itself the model.
senses.example: The model is fine, but our harness drops tool results once the context fills up.

cues.text: An agent keeps losing track of its tool results, and you suspect the code wrapped around the model rather than the model itself.
You are comparing two coding agents that use the same underlying model and want a word for the part that actually differs.
A director asks what your team built if the model came from a vendor, and you want the name for your part.

distractors: An isolated environment where code runs without touching anything real.
The weights of a trained model, stored so it can be loaded again later.
A dashboard that shows how often each model is called and what each call costs.
A written agreement that sets out what a vendor's model may and may not be used for by staff.
The data centre hardware a model runs on, including the chips, memory and cooling it needs.

senses.definition: An isolated place to run something where it cannot affect anything real.
senses.caution: It promises that nothing real can be affected, and compliance teams will hold you to that. It says nothing about how realistic the setup is.
senses.example: Let it run in a sandbox first. I do not want it touching the live index.

cues.text: You are letting an agent execute code it wrote itself and want somewhere it cannot do damage.
Compliance asks what stops the new tool reading customer records during testing.
A vendor wants their engineers to try your pipeline, and you need a word for the walled-off copy you are willing to give them.

distractors: Temporary structure that holds work up until the real thing can stand alone.
A rig that drives a system from outside to see how it behaves.
Present in scattered, isolated places rather than across the whole.
Using your own product for real work before you ask anyone else to.
One of the handful of cloud providers running compute and storage at planetary scale.

senses.gloss: extra help added around a model
gloss_distractors: the prices charged per model call
senses.definition: Extra prompts and checks around a model that help it do a task it cannot do alone.
senses.caution: It implies the extra help can come off as models improve, so people will ask when. Use harness for the code that runs the agent.
senses.example: Most of the gain came from scaffolding: a planning step and a self-check before each answer.

cues.text: A weaker model matched a stronger one once you added a planning step and a self-check, and you want a word for those additions.
A sponsor asks whether the extra prompting steps will still be needed when the next model version ships.
You are explaining that the model did not get smarter, the team gave it a checklist and worked examples to follow.

distractors: Training a model further on examples from one company's own data.
The set of chips and machines that a model runs on in a data centre.
A score that shows how well a model does on a fixed set of test questions.
The written terms that set out who owns what a model produces for each customer that uses it.
A smaller copy of a large model, trained to copy its answers so that it runs more cheaply.
